newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Belgium's painless budget paves way for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Belgium's painless budget paves way for EMU.

text.p: The Belgian government on Friday reached agreement on a 1997 budget designed to pave the way for it to meet the economic targets for European economic and monetary union (EMU) without damaging consumer confidence.

A government source told Reuters on Friday that an 80 billion franc ($2.55 billion) austerity package will cut Belgium's state deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 from an estimated 3.0 percent in 1996.
"There is a full agreement on the budget. We will reach the 2.9 percent target without hurting the average consumer too much," the source said.
Under the Maastricht Treaty, would-be members of a European single currency must meet a deficit target of 3.0 percent of GDP in 1997. Other criteria cover debt and inflation.
Cabinet aides will hammer out the final details of the package over the weekend, after which it will go to a full cabinet session of the centre-left government on Monday.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene will present the full text of the 1997 budget to the Belgian parliament on Tuesday afternoon.
"The three percent norm is reached, that is what financial markets want. And with the exception of beer drinkers, this budget is not going to hurt anyone," said BBL analyst Peter Vanden Houte.
Dehaene appears to have shied away from raising already record-high income tax and radical reform of the country's social security system.
On the taxation side, the 1997 budget hits hard at unhealthy habits -- such as smoking, drinking and driving a car.
On the spending side, Dehaene has made a first stab a reforming Belgium's pension system. With a rapidly ageing population, this is a time bomb for the country's already troubled state finances.

Taxes, mainly indirect, will rise by 30 billion francs. Taxes on petrol will be raised by one franc per litre in October and another franc in January. Taxes on beer will rise by one franc per 25-centilitre bottle, on spirits by 12 francs per 75-centilitre bottle, the source said.
The council of ministers on Friday approved higher excise duties by executive decree. Most will take effect as of October.
The investment world will also have to contribute an estimated five billion francs.
Retail investors will have to pay a 0.3 percent tax on physical delivery of securities by banks and brokerages.
"A small price for anonymity," one analyst said. For tax reasons, many Belgians avoid holding registered securities and prefer holding bearer stocks and bonds in their safes.
Banks will have to pay a 0.06 percent tax on the amount outstanding in savings books accounts, tax-free savings accounts which are Belgium's most popular savings schemes.
The source also said that 50 billion francs of spending cuts had been decided in the social security sector.
The most visible measure is a gradual increase of women's retirement age to 65 years from 60 over a 13-year period, although this will have little impact on the 1997 budget.
The government also decided on a two percent tax on all early retirement pensions.

Most other measures in the social security sector are highly technical. They include a reduction of family allowances for teenagers, a reduction in unemployment benefits for older people and some targeted measures in the health sector. ($1=31.33 Belgian Franc)
